headline: The Iran war dominates the UN General Assembly as Google and OpenAI launch a joint AI safety body — meanwhile the ASX slipped 0.43% but your GOOG and GXAI.AX positions closed higher.

Long-term lithium demand story is intact, but this one needs patience.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS edged up 0.62% today to $539.35, reflecting the broadly flat-to-slightly-positive US session last night. This broad US market ETF is your strongest performer overall at +4.6% — sit tight and let it compound.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG was basically flat today, up a tiny 0.14% to $76.29. No specific news — just a quiet day for this diversified fund. Marginally underwater overall (-0.6%) but well within normal noise for a diversified growth fund.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Bleeding continues — hold or consider topping up?
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is now down 43% on your position and dropped another 2.5% today to $3.84. There's no structural collapse in the company — it's a global lithium price problem as supply has outrun demand. As a long-term holder, the case for lithium in a battery/EV world is still solid. Don't sell into weakness. If you have cash to deploy, this level could be attractive for a long-term top-up — but only if you're comfortable with more short-term pain.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA 6 hype building — sit tight
watch_today.detail: Take-Two slipped 1.6% last night but GTA 6 momentum is building: a Collector's Edition has been revealed, new Rockstar teases are circulating, and 'Cyberleaks' are keeping the title in the news cycle. You're down 12.6% on the position, but the long-term thesis is entirely intact — GTA 6 is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches ever. Hold and wait for the release catalyst.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Positive momentum — stay the course
watch_today.detail: Google is up 1.2% last night and up 10.3% on your position overall. The Gemini 4 early launch reports and Google's co-founding of the SAFA AI safety body with OpenAI and Anthropic both strengthen the long-term story. No reason to do anything here — hold and enjoy the ride.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision watch — could sting property & growth stocks
watch_today.detail: There's active debate this week about whether the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) will lift interest rates at its September meeting. Multiple outlets are covering it today. Higher rates are bad for growth stocks and property values. Your VDHG and GXAI holdings could feel short-term pressure if the RBA hikes. Worth keeping an eye on the announcement.

watch_today.title: Iran war escalating — oil & global markets on edge
watch_today.detail: The Iran conflict is dominating the UN this week. Iran's president says they'll 'fight until the last breath' but has simultaneously offered a 7-day ceasefire. Oil (WTI crude) dropped 1.1% last night to $93.59 — markets aren't panicking yet, but a breakdown in ceasefire talks could spike energy prices fast. Watch oil prices as a canary for escalation risk.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: Good day, improving trend
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF closed up 1.05% today and is getting positive analyst coverage as a top pick for 2027. The launch of a major AI safety standards body (SAFA) by Google, OpenAI and Anthropic signals the industry is maturing — which is actually good for sustained AI investment. Still down 8.2% overall but the trajectory looks better. Hold.

world.summary: The UN General Assembly is the week's centrepiece — Iran, the Middle East, and Trump's foreign policy moves are all front and centre. The Houthi-Saudi conflict is also raising alarm bells for a wider regional war.

stories.title: Iran offers 7-day ceasefire but vows to 'fight until last breath' at UN
stories.why_it_matters: Iran's president told the UN General Assembly that Iran will 'fight until our last breath' — defiant language that signals no easy end to the conflict with the US. At the same time, Iran quietly offered Washington a new 7-day ceasefire proposal, suggesting there's still a diplomatic off-ramp being explored. The US-Iran war is rattling global oil markets (crude is at $93.59/barrel), disrupting shipping, and creating uncertainty across the Middle East. For everyday Australians, sustained conflict means higher fuel prices and broader economic risk.

stories.title: Houthi–Saudi conflict takes on hallmarks of a major Middle Eastern war
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis published today warns that the Houthi-Saudi conflict is rapidly developing the characteristics of a full-scale regional war — sustained aerial campaigns, cross-border strikes, and proxy involvement from Iran. This is separate from but linked to the broader Iran conflict. A wider Middle Eastern war would be catastrophic for global oil supply, with Australia importing significant amounts of refined fuel. It also raises the risk of drawing in Western nations.

stories.title: Netanyahu's UN speech met with protests and diplomatic walkouts
stories.why_it_matters: Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly today and was met with protests in the hall and walkouts by multiple delegations. The scenes reflect deepening global divisions over the Gaza conflict and Israel's broader regional military actions. The diplomatic fallout is significant — it signals growing international isolation of Israel's current government, which complicates US-led efforts to broker any wider Middle East peace deal.

stories.title: Trump accused of interfering in Brazilian elections; illegal voter claims in Nevada collapse
stories.why_it_matters: Democratic lawmakers are accusing the Trump administration of actively interfering in Brazil's upcoming elections — a significant escalation in concerns about US foreign policy overreach. Separately, Trump's claims of 15,000 illegal votes in Nevada have completely unravelled — investigations found zero cases of illegal voting, down from his initial claim of 15,000, then 185, then nothing. Both stories paint a picture of an administration willing to make big claims that don't hold up to scrutiny, which matters for US political stability and international relationships.

stories.title: OECD cuts Turkey's growth forecast to lowest since 2020 due to Iran war fallout
stories.why_it_matters: The OECD (the club of wealthy nations that tracks economic health) has slashed Turkey's growth forecast to its lowest point since 2020, directly citing the impact of the Iran war and rising prices. Turkey is a major regional economy sitting between Europe and the Middle East — when it struggles, the knock-on effects ripple through emerging markets globally. This is a concrete, measurable sign that the Iran conflict is already doing real economic damage beyond the battlefield.

Last night on Wall Street, the S&P 500 was essentially flat (down just 0.02%) and the NASDAQ barely moved (+0.01%). Gold continued its march higher, oil dipped on Iran ceasefire hopes, and the Aussie dollar edged slightly lower against the greenback.

politics.summary: Australian political news today is dominated by two themes: intense debate about whether the RBA will raise interest rates at its September meeting, and the Albanese government quietly reviving its controversial 'misinformation' laws.

stories.title: Will the RBA raise rates in September? Debate intensifies
stories.why_it_matters: There's a serious debate today about whether the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia — the body that sets interest rates) will hike rates at its September board meeting. An ABC analysis asks whether the RBA has already wiped out the home ownership gains that came from recent tax changes — meaning rate rises could undo government housing affordability measures. A University of Sydney paper warns that a single RBA decision can affect home ownership prospects for over a decade. Commercial property is also flagged as increasingly vulnerable if rates rise further. For mortgage holders and property investors, this is the most important domestic economic question right now.

stories.title: The Australian slams RBA for 'covering' Labor's economic failures
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian newspaper is running an opinion piece arguing that the RBA shouldn't effectively 'protect' the Labor government from the consequences of its economic management — suggesting that keeping rates on hold would let Labor off the hook for poor economic policy. This reflects a broader political battle: the Coalition wants to paint Labor as responsible for inflation, while Labor wants the RBA to hold steady. The framing of the RBA as a political shield is increasingly common ahead of the next federal election cycle.

stories.title: Albanese government quietly revives 'misinformation' bill
stories.why_it_matters: Prime Minister Albanese has reportedly put plans to police 'misinformation' back on the agenda, outlined in an unpublished speech. The government's original misinformation bill was shelved after fierce criticism from civil liberties groups and parts of the media who argued it gave government too much power to define what is 'true' online. Reviving it — quietly — will reignite that debate. Critics argue it's a free speech threat; supporters say unchecked misinformation is damaging democracy. Watch for this to become a hot political issue again.

ai.summary: The biggest AI news today is the formal launch of a joint safety standards body — called SAFA — by Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Meanwhile, Google's Gemini 4 is expected to launch earlier than planned, and Australia is pushing for new AI guardrails following a significant OpenAI breach.

stories.title: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic launch joint AI safety body — SAFA
stories.why_it_matters: The three biggest names in AI — Google, OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT), and Anthropic — have jointly announced a new organisation called SAFA (Standards for Artificial Frontier AI) to set safety rules for the most powerful AI systems. This is a significant moment: these companies are fierce competitors, so banding together on safety standards signals they recognise the technology is advancing faster than governments can regulate it. Think of it like car manufacturers agreeing on seatbelt standards before governments mandated them. For investors, it's a sign the AI industry is maturing and trying to get ahead of heavy-handed regulation.

stories.title: Gemini 4 expected to launch early — Google closing the gap on OpenAI
stories.why_it_matters: Reports today suggest Google is preparing to launch Gemini 4 — its next-generation AI model — earlier than originally planned. Google has been seen as playing catch-up to OpenAI's GPT series, and an accelerated Gemini 4 launch would signal Google is serious about reclaiming the lead. For your GOOG holding, this is a positive signal — it means Alphabet's AI investment is translating into real product momentum. A better Gemini also strengthens Google Search and Cloud, which are core revenue drivers.

stories.title: Australia pursues new AI guardrails after 'unprecedented' OpenAI breach
stories.why_it_matters: Australia is moving to tighten AI regulation following what ABC News describes as an 'unprecedented' breach involving OpenAI. While full details of the breach aren't public, the Australian government is reportedly fast-tracking guardrail legislation in response. This matters for Australians because it signals that AI systems handling personal data or sensitive decisions will face new rules — and for investors, it's a reminder that regulatory risk is real for AI companies operating here.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs call for global AI regulation at the UN
stories.why_it_matters: The CEOs of OpenAI (Sam Altman) and Anthropic (Dario Amodei) both spoke at the UN this week, calling for a coordinated global framework to regulate AI. Their key message: AI is advancing so fast that no single country can manage the risks alone, and a global treaty-style approach is needed — similar to how nuclear or chemical weapons are governed. The fact that the companies building the most powerful AI systems are asking to be regulated is unusual and significant — it shows even insiders believe the technology poses genuine risks that need guardrails.

sport.summary: It's Finals Week 3 in the NRL — the Dolphins host the Roosters tonight at Suncorp Stadium, and the Panthers face the Knights on Sunday. The AFL world is in chaos over the Liam Neale trade saga, and there's big Broncos and Roosters team news.

stories.title: Dolphins vs Roosters tonight at Suncorp — but the Roosters are a different beast this finals series
stories.why_it_matters: The Dolphins are 2-0 against the Roosters in regular season this year, but analysts are warning tonight's Roosters are a completely different animal in finals mode. The match kicks off at 7:50pm at Suncorp Stadium — right in your backyard on the Gold Coast. Roosters great (unnamed in available reports) has 'lifted the lid' on coach Trent Robinson's finals mindset, warning the side is peaking at the right time. Should be a cracking Friday night game.

stories.title: Roosters Finals Mail: 'Terribly unlucky' star misses out; secret behind miraculous recovery
stories.why_it_matters: Roosters Late Mail ahead of tonight's final reveals an unnamed star has been 'terribly unlucky' to miss selection in a tough call by coach Robinson. There's also a 'secret' behind one player's miraculous injury recovery that got them up for the game. Roosters are clearly firing on all cylinders heading into tonight — makes the Dolphins' task even harder.

stories.title: Panthers vs Knights on Sunday — ex-Knights star explains why he left Newcastle
stories.why_it_matters: Ahead of Sunday's Preliminary Final at Accor Stadium (Panthers vs Knights), Fox Sports reports a Panthers star has opened up about why he left Newcastle — saying 'I wasn't getting it there.' Wayne Bennett is also pushing his 'Bunker fix' — his long-running campaign to reform the video referee system. The Knights have been a Cinderella story this finals series, so Sunday shapes as a fascinating clash.

stories.title: AFL in uproar over 'utterly shambolic' Liam Neale trade saga
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL world has erupted over what commentators are calling the 'utterly shambolic' handling of Brisbane Lions star Liam Neale's trade request. Multiple pundits said they've 'never been more shocked' by how the situation was managed — the Lions and the receiving club apparently botched the process badly, leaving Neale in limbo. Fox Sports and News.com.au both describe it as a 'total farce.' The AFL trade period always generates drama, but this one is in a different league of dysfunction heading into the off-season.
